query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor alloying addition of boron (≈0.5 at%) to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will segregate at grain boundaries to strengthen intergranular cohesion, thereby increasing the load‐bearing integrity and resistance to cracking while preserving the large field‐ and pressure-induced caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 as produced with a homogeneous, single-phase high‐entropy structure that exhibits large caloric effects but poor fracture toughness (tendency to crack) under load.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled 0.5 atomic percent boron during alloy synthesis so that boron preferentially segregates to the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: The modified and unmodified (control) alloys are processed under identical synthesis and postprocessing conditions, and their performance is evaluated under the same applied magnetic/pressure fields and within the calendric temperature and mechanical load regimes originally used for caloric operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries enhances intergranular bonding and reduces stress concentration sites by mitigating microcrack initiation.
generation.mechanism: The boron atoms at grain boundaries increase cohesion between grains; this improved bonding raises fracture toughness and load-bearing integrity without significantly perturbing the order–disorder transition (and hence the caloric effect) that originates from the bulk matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pristine alloy, the boron-doped alloy will show increased resistance to cracking and an improved fracture toughness under mechanical loading while its externally induced caloric entropy change (caloric response under applied fields and pressure) remains largely unchanged.
generation.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which exhibits a large caloric response but poor mechanical integrity manifested as cracking during load-bearing applications.
generation.boundary: Test conditions are those under which the original caloric performance is evaluated (applied magnetic and pressure fields near the transition temperature, with similar mechanical load limits) so that any changes in integrity can be directly compared.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in fracture toughness and the potential subtle effects of boron on the caloric transition are uncertain and may require adjustment of the boron level to avoid any attenuation of the caloric performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using the same processing route: (a) the control (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, and (b) the modified alloy with 0.5 at% boron added. Evaluate both sets under identical conditions.
measurements: Measure fracture toughness and perform mechanical load tests (e.g., compact tension or bending tests) to assess cracking resistance.
Determine the caloric performance by measuring the entropy change or temperature change under controlled magnetic and pressure-field cycles.
Characterize microstructure (grain boundary chemistry) using electron microscopy and spectroscopy to confirm boron segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fracture toughness (or reduced cracking under load) compared to the control, or if their caloric response (entropy/temperature change) is significantly reduced compared to that of the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
